implementation_notes: On Windows, Message Queuing is the store: MessageQueue.Send writes to a local queue and the MSMQ service forwards to the destination queue when the route is available, storing the message on disk at every hop - Message.Recoverable documents delivery as guaranteed 'even if a computer crashes while the message is en route', and transactional messages are treated as recoverable automatically. The application side is then a local queue name plus a recoverable message, which is the closest a mainstream runtime comes to the pattern being provided out of the box. The hand-written spool remains justified on .NET Core/.NET 5+ (System.Messaging is not part of modern .NET) or when the peer is not another MSMQ host, where an outbox table with FileStream.Flush(true) - or a service-bus client with durable queues - plays the same role.
pitfalls: Recoverable is false by default: an ordinary message lives in memory and is lost if the machine restarts while the peer is still down.
System.Messaging is Windows-only and absent from .NET Core/.NET 5+; a cross-platform service must use an outbox table or a broker client instead.
MessageQueue is IDisposable and depends on the MSMQ service (and the directory service for remote routes); a missing service turns the accept into an exception unless it is handled.
Only payloads the configured formatter can serialise (XmlMessageFormatter-compatible, [Serializable]) can be sent - an incompatible payload fails at accept time, not at delivery time.

variants.name: Outbox table + hosted background relay (.NET, cross-platform)
variants.idiom_name: outbox table + IHostedService relay with FileStream.Flush(true)
variants.implementation_notes: The portable form writes the message into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change and lets a BackgroundService/IHostedService relay poll the table, forward, and delete rows only after the peer acknowledged. Use it when the send must be atomic with a database commit or when MSMQ is unavailable; if the store is a file rather than a table, FileStream.Flush(true) is what makes the write durable, since the parameter flushes intermediate OS buffers and not just the managed buffer. This variant is the mainstream .NET answer on Linux, containers and cloud-hosted services.
pitfalls: FileStream.Flush() without the true argument only clears managed buffers; durability needs Flush(true) or a committed transaction.
A relay that deletes rows before the acknowledgement, or that runs outside the transaction that inserted them, re-creates the dual-write window the outbox exists to close.
Several relay instances must claim rows atomically (UPDATE ... OUTPUT, or SKIP LOCKED on SQL Server/PostgreSQL) or they double-send; polling loops also need backoff.
